{{Short description|Minimal surface in differential geometry}}
[[File:Richmond Surface.png|thumb|Richmond surface for m=2.]]

In [[differential geometry]], a '''Richmond surface''' is a [[minimal surface]] first described by [[Herbert William Richmond]] in 1904.<ref>[[Jesse Douglas]], Tibor Radó, The Problem of Plateau: A Tribute to Jesse Douglas & Tibor Radó, World Scientific, 1992 (p. 239-240)</ref> It is a family of surfaces with one planar [[End (topology)|end]] and one [[Enneper surface]]-like self-intersecting end.

It has [[Weierstrass–Enneper parameterization]] <math>f(z)=1/z^2, g(z)=z^m</math>. This allows a parametrization based on a complex parameter as
:<math>\begin{align}
X(z) &=  \Re[(-1/2z) - z^{2m+1}/(4m+2)]\\
Y(z) &=  \Re[(-i/2z) + i z^{2m+1}/(4m+2)]\\
Z(z) &=  \Re[z^m / m]
\end{align}
</math>
The [[associate family]] of the surface is just the surface rotated around the z-axis.

Taking ''m''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 a real parametric expression becomes:<ref>John Oprea, The Mathematics of Soap Films: Explorations With Maple, American Mathematical Soc., 2000</ref>
:<math>\begin{align}
X(u,v) &= (1/3)u^3 - uv^2 + \frac{u}{u^2+v^2}\\
Y(u,v) &= -u^2v + (1/3)v^3 - \frac{v}{u^2+v^2}\\
Z(u,v) &= 2u
\end{align}
</math>
